survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This factsheet reports PISA 2022 financial literacy results for Spain using the OECD PISA 2022 Database. The assessment is based on sampled schools and students, with students split into two assessment groups (financial literacy plus either mathematics or reading, and the remaining core subjects), so analyses should respect the complex two-stage sampling design. The factsheet does not specify whether analysts applied student/sampling weights or replicate weights; therefore, users of the underlying OECD microdata should apply the official PISA sampling weights and, where available, replicate weights for variance estimation. Because this is a descriptive reporting document (not an ML modeling paper), plausible values and survey design handling should follow OECD PISA technical documentation for financial literacy scaling and standard errors.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is a descriptive OECD factsheet that reports scaled financial literacy outcomes and subgroup comparisons; it does not provide an analysis section describing plausible values (PV) generation/combination or a missing-data strategy. Missing-data handling is therefore not reported in the factsheet because the scaling and PV/missing-data procedures are implemented upstream in the OECD PISA 2022 Database production process rather than re-described here.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample reported for Spain is the set of students who participated in the PISA 2022 financial literacy assessment (the fourth financial literacy cycle). The factsheet does not describe additional exclusions (e.g., missing background questionnaire items or item nonresponse rules) and instead reports the number of students in the financial literacy assessment for Spain.

data.outcome_summary: The OECD PISA 2022 financial literacy assessment (fourth cycle; administered in 2022) measures money-related knowledge and skills for 15-year-old students using a computer-based test. In participating countries/economies, students in sampled schools were split into two groups: one group took the financial literacy assessment and either mathematics or reading, while the other group took the core PISA subjects; both groups were assessed for a total of 120 minutes. Financial literacy items included multiple-choice and constructed-response tasks organized around real-life passages, and students completed a background questionnaire covering attitudes, dispositions, home and school learning experiences, and financial behaviours. For Spain, the factsheet reports an average score of 486 (below the OECD average of 498), with 17% below Level 2 and 5% at Level 5. It also reports that mathematics and reading explain about 76% of variation in financial literacy in Spain, and provides subgroup patterns by gender, socioeconomic status, immigrant background, and several financial education and money-related experiences.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD PISA 2022 factsheet that summarizes descriptive results rather than presenting an original student-level predictive/causal ML analysis. Consequently, fields related to ML techniques, PV combination choices, missing-data handling, and model-based performance metrics are not applicable or not reported within the factsheet itself. The document also does not provide an analytic-methods section specifying weights, PV procedures, or missing-data rules, because these are handled in the OECD PISA database production and scaling pipeline.
